Welcome to Accessible HTML5

This is a well-structured, accessible HTML5 document demonstrating modern best practices for semantic markup and inclusive design.

It uses semantic landmarks, a skip link for keyboard navigation, and CSS that adapts to your light or dark mode preference.

Text and link colors meet WCAG AA contrast in both themes, type scales with your browser's font size, and motion respects your system settings.

Features

  • Semantic HTML structure with proper landmarks
  • Keyboard accessible navigation and focus management
  • Dark mode support with custom color schemes
  • Responsive typography using modern CSS
  • Print-friendly styles for better readability
  • WCAG AA contrast compliance in all color modes

Examples

Component Cards

Card components are useful for organizing related content. They include a subtle border and padding for visual separation.

Learn more about accessibility resources

Interactive Elements

Buttons and links are fully accessible with clear focus states. All interactive elements include visible focus indicators and proper ARIA labels.

Keyboard navigation: Use Tab to move forward, Shift+Tab to move backward, and Enter or Space to activate.

Accessible Form

Click the button to announce a message using a live region. This demonstrates how screen readers are notified of dynamic updates.

This counter demonstrates state management and ARIA live regions for accessible dynamic content. Screen readers announce each change once, from the message below the controls.

content.text:
`0.html` was already in very good shape: accessible, with themes, print styles and form validation all handled well. I made three small changes. I haven't opened the page in a browser or tested it with a screen reader.

1. **Removed the focus jump after the form is sent.** The script used to move focus to the email field after the success message. For screen reader users, the field's announcement could cut off the success message. Focus now stays on the submit button, so the message is read out cleanly.
2. **Fixed the email field's initial error reference.** The field started out pointing at both the hint and an empty error message, in a different order than the script uses later. It now starts with just the hint, and the script adds the error message when there is one.
3. **Gave the "Welcome" section a label.** It now carries a heading-based label like the other sections.

My first try at these edits used a Python script, and the permission check blocked it because this session can't approve prompts. I made the same changes with direct file edits instead.

`0.html` was already in very good shape: accessible, with themes, print styles and form validation all handled well. I made three small changes. I haven't opened the page in a browser or tested it with a screen reader.

1. **Removed the focus jump after the form is sent.** The script used to move focus to the email field after the success message. For screen reader users, the field's announcement could cut off the success message. Focus now stays on the submit button, so the message is read out cleanly.
2. **Fixed the email field's initial error reference.** The field started out pointing at both the hint and an empty error message, in a different order than the script uses later. It now starts with just the hint, and the script adds the error message when there is one.
3. **Gave the "Welcome" section a label.** It now carries a heading-based label like the other sections.

My first try at these edits used a Python script, and the permission check blocked it because this session can't approve prompts. I made the same changes with direct file edits instead.
